profile.name: Adai-adai
profile.tagline: Bruneian coastal dance enacting fishermen at sea and women waiting ashore
profile.insight: In Weston, Sabah and across Brunei, four men and four women perform Adai-adai to the percussion of striking boat hulls and paddles when no instruments are played.
profile.profile: Adai-adai is a traditional dance of the Bruneian Malay ethnic group found in Brunei Darussalam, Sabah, and the Federal Territory of Labuan in Malaysia. The dance portrays coastal community life, depicting a crew of fishermen departing into the sea while women remain on the beach awaiting their return to help gather the catch. Typically performed by a pair of four men and four women, it is accompanied by singing, tambourines, and the gambus lute, or solely by the rhythmic clatter of paddles striking boat hulls and water pitchers. Today it is staged at communal gatherings of the Bruneian Malay people and during official ceremonies to welcome visiting dignitaries.
profile.profile_long:
Adai-adai dance is a traditional dance of the Bruneian Malay ethnic group residing across Brunei Darussalam, Sabah, and the island territory of Labuan in Malaysia. Rooted in maritime livelihood, the performance serves as a vivid narrative of coastal survival and community cooperation. The choreography dramatizes the routine of fishermen who take to open waters to fish, set against the patience and labor of the women who stay behind on the shore, watching the horizon and preparing to receive and sort the catch upon the boats' return.

The dance is traditionally arranged for an ensemble of four men and four women who move together to depict these communal roles. While the specific choreography and footwork counts are not described in sources, the spatial staging reflects the complementary work of maritime life: men enacting the physical navigation and harvesting of the sea, and women welcoming them back along the beach. Its movement vocabulary is performed to vocal melodies whose rhythmic pulse closely mirrors that of Zapin, a widely shared Malay folk tradition across maritime Southeast Asia.

The acoustic framework of Adai-adai is drawn directly from maritime material culture. Musical accompaniment is commonly provided by vocal singing supported by the gambus lute and tambourines. However, in traditional coastal settings, instrumental accompaniment may be entirely absent. In these moments, the singing is propelled purely by work percussion: the striking of wooden paddles against the sides of boats or the rhythmic clatter of the boat hull being paddled, alongside the tapping of water pitchers known as keduit. These sounds evoke the exact sonic environment of sea voyages and shore landings.

Dancers wear colorful special costumes designed for public performance and cultural display. The dance takes place in community spaces during festive crowds and celebrations among the Bruneian Malay community, as well as on formal civic stages to welcome the arrival of dignitaries. Beyond Brunei itself, Adai-adai holds strong geographic roots in northern Borneo, particularly among the Berunai community—the Brunei Malay ethnic group inhabiting the historic settlement of Weston in southwestern Sabah. As a cultural emblem, it preserves the coastal narrative of Borneo's maritime communities across modern administrative borders.

sections.origins_and_history: Adai-adai is a traditional dance of the Bruneian Malay ethnic group originating along the coasts of Brunei Darussalam, Sabah, and Labuan in Malaysia. Rooted in coastal subsistence, it developed as a narrative expression reflecting the life and labor of local fishermen and their communities. It is recognized as a tribal dance of the Berunai—the Brunei Malay population inhabiting the coastal town of Weston in Sabah.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed by an ensemble typically composed of a pair of four men and four women. The staging reenacts maritime labor, telling the story of fishermen journeying out to sea while women wait along the beach to help collect and handle the landed catch. Specific footwork, hand gestures, and counts are not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: Adai-adai is accompanied by singing delivered with a rhythm almost similar to the Zapin dance rhythm. Melodic and percussive accompaniment is provided by the gambus (plucked lute) and tambourines. Alternatively, the dance can be accompanied entirely without formal musical instruments; in such cases, singing is sustained by the sound of paddlers striking the sides of the boat or hull during paddling, alongside the rhythmic striking of a water pitcher or keduit.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear colorful special costumes suited to cultural presentations. Performances occur in community settings, public gatherings, and event spaces across Brunei, Sabah, and Labuan.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance expresses the reciprocal life of coastal families, symbolizing the journey of seafaring providers and the supportive community awaiting them on shore. It is customarily staged during communal gatherings of the Bruneian Malay community and during formal events to welcome visiting dignitaries.
sections.regional_variants: In Sabah, Adai-adai is preserved and performed specifically by the Berunai (Brunei Malay ethnic group) living in the coastal town of Weston.
sections.lineage: Adai-adai belongs to the Bruneian Malay folk heritage of northwestern Borneo, sharing stylistic and rhythmic affinities with the wider Malay Zapin tradition.

episode_brief.logline: On the shores of Sabah and Brunei, eight dancers reenact the daily hazards of ocean fishermen to the percussive strike of oars against boat timbers.
beats: Open along the water in Weston, Sabah, where local Berunai elders gather by wooden boats.
Demonstrate the acoustic percussion: striking wooden paddles against the hull and tapping the keduit pitcher.
The four male dancers assemble to represent the fishing crew departing across open water.
The four female dancers line the shore, enacting the vigil and the eventual sorting of the catch.
The full ensemble reunites to demonstrate the complete Zapin-like cadence used to welcome dignitaries.

lesson_ladder.goal: Execute the full narrative cycle from departure to landing
drills: Integrate sung accompaniment with paddle-stroke rhythms
Transition into the gathering and welcoming sequence
